title: Expression Syntax
learning_outcomes: Explain the key behavior of expression syntax and identify when it should be used.
Configure or review the workflow fields and permissions relevant to expression syntax.
Verify the result using a controlled run or static check and interpret the evidence.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on expression syntax. Expressions use `${{ ... }}` to read contexts, compare values, and build conditional configuration; their evaluation timing differs from shell variable expansion. Use the example to predict the workflow result, then verify the behavior in a safe test repository or by static review.
content.why_it_matters: Expression Syntax matters because it affects correctness, security, maintainability, or operating cost. Expressions use `${{ ... }}` to read contexts, compare values, and build conditional configuration; their evaluation timing differs from shell variable expansion. Contexts, environment variables, and expressions have different scopes and evaluation times. Treat event data as untrusted and avoid interpolating untrusted values directly into shell source.

items.text: YAML is indentation-sensitive. Check that nested values are aligned, values have the expected type, special strings are quoted when needed, and the workflow schema accepts the key at that level.

items.title: Expression evaluation timing
items.text: Use `${{ ... }}` for workflow expressions and the correct context for the field. Treat event-derived values as data: pass untrusted text through an environment variable and quote it instead of inserting it into shell source.

content_blocks.code:
jobs:
  validate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Validate input and exit status"
  report:
    needs: validate
    if: ${{ always() }}
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: echo "Inspect the dependency result before acting"
content_blocks.expected_output: The reporting job waits for the validation job and runs even after it finishes; real cleanup/reporting logic should inspect `needs.validate.result` before making decisions.

content_blocks.text: Inspect the example and make one focused change related to expression syntax. Predict the expected result first, then use the run instructions or a static review to check it. content_blocks.title: Recap
content_blocks.text: You should now be able to explain expression syntax, read the example, and identify a way to validate it. The wider system goal remains: Pass explicit values between workflow components while treating event data as untrusted input.

content.task: Apply expression syntax to a small workflow change. State the expected result first, validate the configuration, then record evidence from the run or static check.

content.expected_output: The expected result is the behavior described here: Expressions use `${{ ... }}` to read contexts, compare values, and build conditional configuration; their evaluation timing differs from shell variable expansion. The real result depends on the repository, selected ref, configured permissions, and runner availability.
troubleshooting: If a workflow never starts, verify the workflow is under `.github/workflows/`, the event and filters match, and repository/organization Actions policy allows it.
If a step fails, inspect the first failed step, exit code, stderr, installed tool versions, permissions, and runner/network state before retrying.
If a job is skipped or data is missing, inspect `if`, `needs`, outputs, artifact names/paths, and cache keys; jobs do not automatically share filesystems.
common_mistakes: Assuming YAML parsing proves the workflow runs correctly or matches the intended trigger.
Granting broad token permissions, printing environment values, or exposing a secret to untrusted code.
Using a placeholder command as evidence of a real build, test, deployment, or security scan.
